## Learning Objectives

:::{style="font-size: .8em"}
- Review vector spaces and subspaces 
- Column space: what outputs can $A$ produce?
- Null space: what inputs does $A$ collapse to zero?
- Key distinction: Col $A \subseteq \mathbb{R}^m$ vs Nul $A \subseteq \mathbb{R}^n$
- Motivating question: can we solve $A\mathbf{x} = \mathbf{b}$ for housing prices?

:::

## What is a Vector Space?

```{python}
from IPython.core.display import HTML
display(HTML(r"""
<div class="blue-box">
    <p><b>Definition:</b> What is a vector space? What are the key properties it must satisfy?</p>
    <p><b>Examples:</b> Can you think of some examples of vector spaces? What about non-examples?</p>
</div>
"""))
```

## Vector Space Example{.smaller-title}

<!-- super special rare .55 em appearance to get text all in one line. -->
:::{style="font-size: .7em"}
Example of a vector space:
$$\mathbb{R}^2 = \left\{ \begin{bmatrix}a_1\\ a_2\end{bmatrix}\text{ such that } a_1, a_2 \in \mathbb{R} \right\}$$
with usual addition and scalar multiplication.

The above notation tells us that $\mathbb{R}^2$ consists of all vectors with two real components.

$$
\begin{bmatrix}
    1 \\ 2
\end{bmatrix}, \begin{bmatrix}
    -41 \\ \frac{3}{5}
\end{bmatrix},
\begin{bmatrix}
    \sqrt{2} \\ -\pi
\end{bmatrix},
\begin{bmatrix}
    0 \\ 1
\end{bmatrix},
\begin{bmatrix}
    0 \\ 0
\end{bmatrix}\in \mathbb{R}^2
$$

:::


## Vector Space Definition{.smaller-title}

:::{style="font-size: .7em"}
```{python}
from IPython.core.display import HTML

def generate_html():
    return r"""
    <div class="purple-box">
        <span class="label">Vector Space</span>
        <p>
        A <b>vector space</b> is a set of vectors together with rules for vector addition and scalar multiplication. The set of vectors must be <em>closed</em> under these two operations. And the eight conditions listed below must be satisfied.
        
        <ol>
        <li> \(\mathbf{x} + \mathbf{y} = \mathbf{y} + \mathbf{x}\)</li>
        <li> \(\mathbf{x} + (\mathbf{y} + \mathbf{z}) = (\mathbf{x}+\mathbf{y})+\mathbf{z}\)</li>
        <li> There is a unique "zero" vector such that \(\mathbf{x}+\mathbf{0} = \mathbf{x}\) for all \(\mathbf{x}\)</li>
        <li> For each \(\mathbf{x}\) there is a unique vector \(-\mathbf{x}\) such that \(\mathbf{x}+(-\mathbf{x})=\mathbf{0}\)</li>
        <li> 1 times \(\mathbf{x}\) equals \(\mathbf{x}\)</li>
        <li> \((c_1c_2)\mathbf{x} = c_1(c_2\mathbf{x})\)</li>
        <li> \(c(\mathbf{x}+\mathbf{y}) = c\mathbf{x}+c\mathbf{y}\)</li>
        <li> \((c_1+c_2)\mathbf{x} = c_1\mathbf{x}+c_2\mathbf{x}\)</li>
        </ol>
        </p>
    </div>
    """

html_content = generate_html()
display(HTML(html_content))
```
:::

## Definition: Subspaces{.smaller-title}

:::{style="font-size: .7em"}

```{python}
from IPython.core.display import HTML

def generate_html():
    return r"""
    <div class="purple-box">
        <span class="label">Euclidean Subspace</span>
        <p>
        A <b>subspace of</b> \(\mathbb{R}^n\) is any set \(H\) of vectors in \(\mathbb{R}^n\) that satisfies three properties:
        <ol start="1">
        <li> The zero vector is in \(H\).</li>
        <li> For each \(\mathbf{u}\) and \(\mathbf{v}\) in \(H\), the sum \(\mathbf{u} + \mathbf{v}\) is in \(H\) (\(H\) is closed under addition).</li>
        <li>For each \(\mathbf{u}\) in \(H\) and each scalar \(c,\) the vector \(c\mathbf{u}\) is in \(H\) (\(H\) is closed under scalar multiplication).</li>
    </div>
    """
html_content = generate_html()
display(HTML(html_content))
```


:::{.fragment}
Each subspace is a vector space in its own right.
```{python}
def generate_html():
    return r"""
    <div class="blue-box">
        <p>Why is it enough to show these three properties?</p>
    </div><br>
    """
display(HTML(generate_html()))
```
:::

:::{.fragment}
```{python}
def generate_html():
    return r"""
    <div class="blue-box">
        <p>Is \(\mathbb{R}^2\) a subspace of \(\mathbb{R}^3\)?</p>
    </div>
    """
display(HTML(generate_html()))
```
:::
:::

## Every Span Is a Subspace{.smaller-title}

:::{style="font-size:.8em"}
__Example.__ Take $\mathbf{v}_1$ and $\mathbf{v}_2$ in $\mathbb{R}^n$,  and let $H$ = Span$\{\mathbf{v}_1, \mathbf{v}_2\}.$ 
Then $H$ is a subspace of $\mathbb{R}^n$.

:::{.center-text}
```{python}
import laUtilities as ut
qr_setting = None
import numpy as np

fig = ut.three_d_figure((7, 1), fig_desc = 'Span{v1, v2}, a subspace.',
                        xmin = -10, xmax = 10, ymin = -10, ymax = 10, zmin = -10, zmax = 10, qr = qr_setting)
a1 = [-8.0, 8.0, 5.0]
a2 = [3.0,  2.0, -2.0]
a3 = 2.5 * np.array(a2)
fig.text(a1[0]+.5, a1[1]+.5, a1[2]+.5, r'$\bf v_1$', 'v_1', size=20)
fig.text(a3[0]+.5, a3[1]+.5, a3[2]+.5, r'$\bf v_2$', 'v_2', size=20)
fig.plotSpan(a1, a2,'Green')
fig.plotPoint(a1[0], a1[1], a1[2],'r')
fig.plotPoint(a3[0], a3[1], a3[2],'r')
# fig.plotPoint(a3[0], a3[1], a3[2],'r')
#fig.text(a1[0], a1[1], a1[2], r'$\bf v_1$', 'a_1', size=20)
fig.text(0.1, 0.1, -3, r'$\bf 0$', '0', size=12)
fig.plotPoint(0, 0, 0, 'b')
fig.set_title(r'Span{$v_1, v_2$}, a subspace.')
fig.text(9, -9, -7, r'$\bf H$', 'H', size = 20)
```
:::
Let us see why $H$ satisfies the definition of a subspace.
:::

## Subspaces Are Closed Under Addition{.really-smaller-title}

:::{style="font-size: .8em"}
__Example (continued).__

 __Property 1.__ The zero vector is in $H$.

:::{.fragment}
$$
{\bf 0} = 0\mathbf{v}_1 + 0\mathbf{v}_2\text{ is in Span}\{\mathbf{v}_1, \mathbf{v}_2\}.
$$
:::

:::{.fragment}


__Property 2.__ For any two vectors ${\bf u}, {\bf v} \in H$, their sum is also in $H$.
:::

:::{.fragment}
If $\mathbf{u} = s_1\mathbf{v}_1 + s_2\mathbf{v}_2,$ and $\mathbf{v} = t_1\mathbf{v}_1 + t_2\mathbf{v}_2,$ then their sum
$$
\mathbf{u} + \mathbf{v} = (s_1+t_1)\mathbf{v}_1 + (s_2+t_2)\mathbf{v}_2 \in H.
$$
:::
:::

## Subspaces Are Closed Under Scalar Multiplication{.really-smaller-title}

:::{style="font-size: .8em"}

__Property 3.__ For any vector ${\bf u} \in H$ and scalar $c \in \mathbb{R}$, the vector $c\mathbf{u}$ is in $H$.

:::{.fragment}
$$
c\mathbf{u} = c(s_1\mathbf{v}_1 + s_2\mathbf{v}_2) = (cs_1\mathbf{v}_1 + cs_2\mathbf{v}_2) \in H.
$$
:::

:::{.fragment}
```{python}
def generate_html():
    return r"""
    <div class="blue-box">
        <p>We showed every span is a subspace. Is the converse true? Is every subspace a span of some set of vectors?</p>
    </div>
    """
display(HTML(generate_html()))
```
:::
:::

## Definition: Column Space{.smaller-title}

:::{style="font-size: .8em"}
Every matrix has associated with it two vector spaces:  _**column space**_ and  _**null space.**_ 


```{python}
def generate_html():
    return r"""
    <div class="purple-box">
        <p> <span class="label">Column space</span>
         The <b>column space</b> of a matrix \(A\) is the set \({\operatorname{Col}}\ A\) of all linear combinations of the columns of \(A\).
        </p>
    </div>
    """
html_content = generate_html()
display(HTML(html_content))
```

The column space of an $m\times n$ matrix is a subspace of...


:::{.fragment}
 $\mathbb{R}^m.$  If $A$ = $[\mathbf{a}_1 \;\cdots\; \mathbf{a}_n]$, with columns in $\mathbb{R}^m,$ then ${\operatorname{Col}}\ A$ is the same as $\text{Span}\{\mathbf{a}_1,\dots,\mathbf{a}_n\}$. Hence, ${\operatorname{Col}}\ A$ is a subspace of $\mathbb{R}^m$ and a vector space.
:::


:::{.fragment}
Note that ${\operatorname{Col}}\ A$ equals $\mathbb{R}^m$ only when the columns of $A$ span $\mathbb{R}^m.$  Otherwise, ${\operatorname{Col}}\ A$ is only part of $\mathbb{R}^m.$
:::

:::{.fragment}
```{python}
from IPython.core.display import HTML

def generate_html():
    return r"""
    <div class="blue-box">
        <p>If \(A\) is a \(3\times 4\) matrix, what vector space does \(\operatorname{Col} A\) live in? What are the possible dimensions of \(\operatorname{Col} A\)?</p>
    </div>
    """
display(HTML(generate_html()))
```
:::
:::

## Column Space and Linear Transformations{.really-smaller-title}

:::{style="font-size: .8em"}
_**Algebraic view**_: for a linear system $A\mathbf{x} = \mathbf{b}$, ${\operatorname{Col}}\ A$ is the set of all $\mathbf{b}$ for which the system has a solution. 

<br>

:::{.fragment}
_**Geometric view**_: for  linear transformation $T: \mathbb{R}^n\rightarrow\mathbb{R}^m$ with standard matrix $A$, ${\operatorname{Col}}\ A$ is the _range_ of $T.$

:::{.center-text}
```{python}
fig = ut.three_d_figure((7, 3), fig_desc = 'Column Space of A = [a1, a2, a3].',
                        xmin = -10, xmax = 10, ymin = -10, ymax = 10, zmin = -10, zmax = 10, qr = qr_setting)
a1 = [-8.0, 8.0, 5.0]
a2 = [3.0,  2.0, -2.0]
a3 = 2.5 * np.array(a2)
fig.text(a1[0]+.5, a1[1]+.5, a1[2]+.5, r'$\bf a_1$', 'a_1', size=18)
fig.text(a3[0]+.5, a3[1]+.5, a3[2]+.5, r'$\bf a_3$', 'a_3', size=18)
fig.text(a2[0]+.5, a2[1]+.5, a2[2]+.5, r'$\bf a_2$', 'a_2', size=18)
fig.plotSpan(a1, a2,'Green')
fig.plotPoint(a1[0], a1[1], a1[2],'r')
fig.plotPoint(a3[0], a3[1], a3[2],'r')
fig.plotPoint(a2[0], a2[1], a2[2],'r')
# fig.plotPoint(a3[0], a3[1], a3[2],'r')
fig.text(0.1, 0.1, -3, r'$\bf 0$', '0', size=12)
fig.plotPoint(0, 0, 0, 'b')
fig.set_title(r'Column Space of $A = [{\bf a}_1, {\bf a}_2, {\bf a}_3]$')
fig.text(9, -9, -7, r'Col $A$', 'H', size = 16)
```
:::
:::
:::

## Column Space in Data Science{.smaller-title}

:::{style="font-size: .7em"}
For our housing dataset, $A$ is the $6 \times 3$ design matrix (intercept, sqft, bedrooms) and $\mathbf{b}$ is the price vector:

$$
A = \begin{bmatrix}1 & 800 & 1\\1 & 1150 & 2\\1 & 1500 & 2\\1 & 1800 & 3\\1 & 2100 & 3\\1 & 2450 & 4\end{bmatrix}, \quad
\mathbf{b} = \begin{bmatrix}118\\157\\193\\236\\264\\312\end{bmatrix}.
$$

- **$\operatorname{Col} A$** is the set of all price vectors our model can *possibly* produce (the "reachable outputs").
- $\mathbf{b} \in \operatorname{Col} A$ only if the data falls *exactly* on a linear surface, which is almost never true with real measurements.
- When $\mathbf{b} \notin \operatorname{Col} A$ we need a best approximation. That's where least squares comes in (L25).
:::

## Definition: Null Space{.smaller-title}

:::{style="font-size: .8em"}
```{python}
def generate_html():
    return r"""
    <div class="purple-box">
        <p>  <span class="label">Null space</span>
         The <b>null space</b> (or  <b>kernel</b>) of a matrix \(A\) is the set \({\operatorname{Nul}}\ A\) of all solutions of the <i>homogeneous</i> equation \(A \bf{x} = 0\).
        </p>
    </div>
    """
html_content = generate_html()
display(HTML(html_content))
```

:::{.fragment}
_**Geometric view**_: the set of all vectors that are mapped to the zero vector by $A$.
:::

:::{.fragment}
_**Algebraic view**_: the set of all solutions of $A\mathbf{x} = {\bf 0}$.


When $A$ has $n$ columns, a solution of $A\mathbf{x} = {\bf 0}$ is a vector in $\mathbb{R}^n$. Hence, the null space of $A$ is a subset of $\mathbb{R}^n$.

To test whether a vector $\mathbf{v}$ is in ${\operatorname{Nul}}\ A$, simply compute $A\mathbf{v}$ and see if the result is zero.
:::

:::

## Null Space Is a Subspace of R^n{.smaller-title}

:::{style="font-size: .8em"}
```{python}
def generate_html():
    return r"""
    <div class="purple-box">
        <p>  <span class="label">Theorem</span>
         The null space of an \(m\times n\) matrix \(A\) is a subspace of \(\mathbb{R}^n\).   

Equivalently, the set of all solutions of a system \(A\mathbf{x} = {\bf 0}\) of \(m\) homogeneous linear equations in \(n\) unknowns is a subspace of \(\mathbb{R}^n.\)
        </p>
    </div>
    """
html_content = generate_html()
display(HTML(html_content))
```

:::{.fragment}
```{python}

    </div>
    """
display(HTML(generate_html()))
```

:::


## Null Space Is a Subspace of R^n{.smaller-title}

:::{style="font-size: .8em"}
```{python}
def generate_html():
    return r"""
    <div class="purple-box">
        <p>  <span class="label">Theorem</span>
         The null space of an \(m\times n\) matrix \(A\) is a subspace of \(\mathbb{R}^n\).   

Equivalently, the set of all solutions of a system \(A\mathbf{x} = {\bf 0}\) of \(m\) homogeneous linear equations in \(n\) unknowns is a subspace of \(\mathbb{R}^n.\)
        </p>
    </div>
    """
html_content = generate_html()
display(HTML(html_content))
```


__Proof.__ To prove this theorem, we must show that ${\operatorname{Nul}}\ A$ satisfies the 3 properties of a subspace.
<br><br>


:::{.fragment}
_Property 1._ The zero vector is in ${\operatorname{Nul}}\ A$.
:::

:::{.fragment}
&emsp;&emsp;We can calculate the matrix-vector product 
$$
A{\bf 0} = 0 \cdot {\bf a_1} + 0 \cdot {\bf a_2} + \cdots + 0 \cdot {\bf a_n} = {\bf 0}.
$$
:::
:::


## Proof: Null Space Is a Subspace{.smaller-title}

:::{style="font-size: .8em"}
_Property 2._ The sum of two vectors in ${\operatorname{Nul}}\ A$ is in ${\operatorname{Nul}}\ A.$

:::{.fragment}
&emsp;&emsp;Take two vectors $\mathbf{u}$ and $\mathbf{v}$ that are in ${\operatorname{Nul}}\ A.$  

&emsp;&emsp;By definition $A\mathbf{u} = {\bf 0}$ and $A\mathbf{v} = {\bf 0}.$

&emsp;&emsp;Then $\mathbf{u} + \mathbf{v}$ is in ${\operatorname{Nul}}\ A$ because 
$$
A(\mathbf{u} + \mathbf{v}) = A\mathbf{u} + A\mathbf{v} = {\bf 0} + {\bf 0} = {\bf 0}.
$$
<br>
:::

:::{.fragment}
_Property 3._ Any scalar multiple of a vector in ${\operatorname{Nul}}\ A$ is in ${\operatorname{Nul}}\ A.$
:::


:::{.fragment}
&emsp;&emsp;Take a vector $\mathbf{v}$ that is in ${\operatorname{Nul}}\ A.$  Then $A(c\mathbf{v}) = cA\mathbf{v} = c{\bf 0} = {\bf 0}.$
:::


:::{.fragment}
```{python}
def generate_html():
    return r"""
    <div class="blue-box">
        <p>If \(A\) is an invertible \(n \times n\) matrix, what is \(\operatorname{Nul} A\)? Why?</p>
    </div>
    """
display(HTML(generate_html()))
```
:::
:::

## What do Null Spaces Mean for Data?{.really-smaller-title}

:::{style="font-size: .8em"}
Suppose bedrooms $=$ sqft$/600$ (a perfectly redundant feature):

```{python}
import numpy as np, pandas as pd

sqft  = np.array([800., 1150., 1500., 1800., 2100., 2450.])
beds  = sqft / 600   # perfectly collinear
price = np.array([118., 157., 193., 236., 264., 312.])

df = pd.DataFrame({'sqft': sqft.astype(int),
                   'beds (= sqft/600)': beds.round(2),
                   'price ($k)': price.astype(int)})
print(df.to_string(index=False))
```

Now consider two very different models: $\hat{\boldsymbol{\beta}}_1 = [10,\ 0.10,\ 20]$ and $\hat{\boldsymbol{\beta}}_2 = [10,\ 1.10,\ -580]$ (raise the sqft coefficient by 1, drop the bedrooms coefficient by 600).

```{python}
A = np.column_stack([np.ones(6), sqft, beds])

beta1 = np.array([10.,    0.10,   20.])
beta2 = np.array([10.,    1.10, -580.])   # beta1 + [0, +1, -600]

print("β₁ predictions:", (A @ beta1).round(1))
print("β₂ predictions:", (A @ beta2).round(1))
```

**Identical predictions, so the direction $[0,\ {+1},\ {-600}]$ is in $\operatorname{Nul} A$.** 

The model can shift weight freely between sqft and bedrooms without affecting anything it can measure. That's why collinear features make coefficients meaningless.

_L21 quantifies exactly how many such directions exist. That's the rank._
:::

## Col A and Nul A Live in Different Spaces{.really-smaller-title}

:::{style="font-size: .8em"}
Note that the two subspaces ${\operatorname{Col}}\ A$ and ${\operatorname{Nul}}\ A$ live in different "universes."

For an $m\times n$ matrix, 

* the column space is a subset of the codomain $\mathbb{R}^m$,
* while the null space is a subset of the domain $\mathbb{R}^n$.

```{python}
from IPython.core.display import HTML

def generate_html():
    return r"""
    <div class="blue-box">
        <p>For a \(3\times 5\) matrix \(A\), what is the ambient vector space for \(\operatorname{Col} A\)? For \(\operatorname{Nul} A\)? Could a vector belong to both?</p>
    </div>
    """
display(HTML(generate_html()))
```
:::

## Col A and Nul A in Their Spaces{.really-smaller-title}

:::{.center-text}
```{python}
import matplotlib.pyplot as plt
import matplotlib.patches as mpatches

fig, ax = plt.subplots(figsize=(10, 3.5))
ax.set_xlim(0, 10)
ax.set_ylim(0, 4)
ax.axis('off')

# Left box: R^n (domain)
left_box = mpatches.FancyBboxPatch((0.2, 0.3), 3.6, 3.2,
    boxstyle="round,pad=0.1", linewidth=2, edgecolor='steelblue', facecolor='#e8f4f8')
ax.add_patch(left_box)
ax.text(2.0, 3.25, r'$\mathbb{R}^n$  (domain)', ha='center', fontsize=14,
        fontweight='bold', color='steelblue')

# Nul A oval
nul_oval = mpatches.Ellipse((2.0, 1.6), 2.4, 1.8, linewidth=1.5,
    edgecolor='blue', facecolor='gray', alpha=0.6)
ax.add_patch(nul_oval)
ax.text(2.0, 1.6, r'Nul $A$', ha='center', va='center', fontsize=13, color='navy')

# Arrow from left to right
ax.annotate('', xy=(6.9, 1.7), xytext=(3.9, 1.7),
    arrowprops=dict(arrowstyle='->', color='black', lw=2.5))
ax.text(5.0, 2.35, r'$A$', ha='center', fontsize=18, fontstyle='italic')

# Right box: R^m (codomain)
right_box = mpatches.FancyBboxPatch((6.2, 0.3), 3.6, 3.2,
    boxstyle="round,pad=0.1", linewidth=2, edgecolor='darkgreen', facecolor='#eef8ee')
ax.add_patch(right_box)
ax.text(8.0, 3.25, r'$\mathbb{R}^m$  (codomain)', ha='center', fontsize=14,
        fontweight='bold', color='darkgreen')

# Col A oval
col_oval = mpatches.Ellipse((8.0, 1.6), 2.4, 1.8, linewidth=1.5,
    edgecolor='green', facecolor='lightgreen', alpha=0.6)
ax.add_patch(col_oval)
ax.text(8.0, 1.6, r'Col $A$', ha='center', va='center', fontsize=13, color='darkgreen')

plt.tight_layout()
```
:::

:::{style="font-size: .8em"}
For an $m\times n$ matrix: $\operatorname{Nul} A \subset \mathbb{R}^n$ and $\operatorname{Col} A \subset \mathbb{R}^m.$ These live in entirely different spaces.
:::

## Looking Ahead{.smaller-title}

:::{style="font-size: .7em"}
We've introduced two fundamental subspaces of any matrix $A$:

- **$\operatorname{Col} A \subset \mathbb{R}^m$**: the reachable outputs. Whether $\mathbf{b} \in \operatorname{Col} A$ determines if $A\mathbf{x} = \mathbf{b}$ is solvable.
- **$\operatorname{Nul} A \subset \mathbb{R}^n$**: the invisible inputs. A nontrivial null space signals redundant or collinear features.

In the next lectures we build the tools to characterize these spaces more precisely:

| Lecture | Topic | DS Payoff |
|------|---------|-----------|
| L21 | Basis & Dimension | How many truly independent features? |
| L22 | Coordinate Systems | Representing data in a new basis |
| L23–24 | Projection & QR | Best approximation when $\mathbf{b} \notin \operatorname{Col} A$ |
| L25–26 | Least Squares & Regression | Fitting models to noisy data |
:::
